trainings.summaryHtml: A practical field training for wiring readers, locks, exit buttons, emergency release, and controller inputs before handover.

sections.heading: Controller and Lock Wiring
sections.paragraph: Start by separating controller power, lock power, reader data, request-to-exit, and emergency release wiring. This makes troubleshooting easier and protects the controller from lock surge issues.
Before the door is closed for final testing, trigger every input manually and confirm the event appears correctly in the software. This catches swapped wires and wrong door numbers early.

sections.heading: Handover Test
sections.paragraph: Finish by testing card access, PIN access if available, exit button behavior, fire release behavior, and fail-safe or fail-secure lock response. Record the results in the handover document.

trainings.title: Access Control Door Wiring and Testing
trainings.summary: A practical field training for wiring readers, locks, exit buttons, emergency release, and controller inputs before handover.

trainings.summaryHtml: Training for IP address planning, camera activation, stream settings, naming, NVR recording, and final view checks.

sections.heading: Network and Naming Plan
sections.paragraph: Prepare the IP range, gateway, password standard, camera naming convention, and NVR channel map before activation. A small plan saves a lot of site time.
After the camera is online, check day view, night view, angle, focus, motion detection, recording schedule, and remote access from the client account.

blogs.summaryHtml: A practical guide for consultants and contractors to reserve pathways, power, rack space, and device locations before site work becomes expensive.

sections.heading: Start With Pathways
sections.paragraph: Reserve cable trays, conduits, sleeves, risers, and rack routes early. CCTV, access control, intercom, Wi-Fi, audio, and fire systems all become easier when the cable path is designed before construction begins.

A simple coordination drawing can prevent many site problems. It should show rack location, power availability, device points, network uplinks, containment routes, and spare capacity for future expansion.

sections.heading: Leave Space for Growth
sections.paragraph: A rack that is full on day one becomes difficult to maintain. Add spare patch panel ports, switch ports, UPS capacity, and cable management space so the system can grow without messy rework.

blogs.title: How to Plan ELV Systems Before Construction Starts
blogs.summary: A practical guide for consultants and contractors to reserve pathways, power, rack space, and device locations before site work becomes expensive.
blogs.body: Good ELV planning starts before walls are closed and ceilings are installed.

blogs.summaryHtml: Camera selection should be based on distance, light, angle, mounting height, analytics need, and recording purpose rather than megapixels alone.

sections.heading: Megapixels Are Not the Whole Answer
sections.paragraph: A high-resolution camera can still perform badly if the lens angle, lighting, mounting point, and target distance are wrong. Start with the viewing objective, then select the camera type.

sections.heading: Night View and WDR
sections.paragraph: Entrances, glass doors, parking ramps, and warehouse shutters often need stronger wide dynamic range or low-light capability. Test the actual scene whenever possible before final approval.

blogs.title: Choosing the Right Camera for Real Site Conditions
blogs.summary: Camera selection should be based on distance, light, angle, mounting height, analytics need, and recording purpose rather than megapixels alone.
blogs.body: Megapixels matter, but the site condition decides the correct camera.

blogs.summaryHtml: Small wiring and hardware decisions can create daily access problems. This article explains the checks that matter before handover.

sections.heading: Wrong Lock Type
sections.paragraph: Fail-safe and fail-secure locks behave differently during power loss and emergency release. Confirm the safety requirement before choosing magnetic locks, strikes, bolts, or electric handles.

sections.heading: Reader Position
sections.paragraph: Readers should be mounted at a comfortable height and away from metal interference where possible. Poor placement makes daily use frustrating even when the controller is working correctly.
Final testing should include card access, exit button behavior, door forced alarm, door held open alarm, emergency release, and software event logs.

blogs.title: Common Access Control Door Mistakes
blogs.summary: Small wiring and hardware decisions can create daily access problems. This article explains the checks that matter before handover.
blogs.body: Most access control issues are avoidable with a clean door checklist.

blogs.summaryHtml: A text-focused field note for rack labeling, patching, switch access, documentation, and maintenance readiness.

sections.heading: Label Everything
sections.paragraph: Patch panel ports, switch ports, uplinks, UPS outputs, and device cables should follow one naming method. Labels save hours during troubleshooting and future additions.
Keep a printed or digital port map with the rack. Include switch IP addresses, VLAN notes, uplink paths, spare ports, and the latest as-built drawing reference.
